Part III: DuPont Analysis: Apply appropriate data analytic techniques

Background

The data for this case was extracted from company financial statements posted online from credible sources. Many of the transformations has been done for you as well. Balance sheet data and income statement data were in separate files and have been matched by company and year into a single file. The resulting file is a comma separated values (csv) file, dupont-analysis-combined.csv, that is ready to be loaded into R. You will be need to compute the ratios involved in the DuPont Method once it has been loaded into R.

The student is required to check data to make certain values are within expected ranges and are valid.

Financial Statment Import

This project’s data contains the financial ratios for the DOW-30 companies.

Data Understanding & Cleaning

A. While the instructor is responsible for properly loading the data from the file; you as the analyst are responsible for the data understanding (CRISP-DM-I) and business understanding (CRISP-DM-II). Review the four primary ratios that we will be examining for the DuPont Analysis.

  • Some questions you should consider are: is the value of the expected data type (Integer, Decimal/Float, Categorical)?
  • Can you recalculate this number and cross check it is given to you properly?
  • Is the numeric sign (+/-) as you expect?
  • For ratios, should the value be inverted (1/x)?

In the end, calculate the correct ratios based on the financial statement data and store with an appended _calc. (ROE_calc, ProfitMargin_calc, AssetTurnover_calc, FinancialLeverage_calc, and any additional data you deem necessary). Make certain that no infinite values sneak in as these will cause calculation problems for mean and standard deviation.

Question A, Student 
duPont <- duPont %>%
  mutate(ROE_calc = round(NetIncome/ShareholderEquity , 4),
         ProfitMargin_calc = round(NetIncome / NetRevenues, 4),
         AssetTurnover_calc = round(NetRevenues / TotalAssets, 4),
         FinancialLeverage_calc = round(TotalAssets / ShareholderEquity, 4)) %>%
  
  mutate(ROE_calc = ifelse(is.finite(ROE_calc), ROE_calc, NA),
         ProfitMargin_calc = ifelse(is.finite(ProfitMargin_calc), ProfitMargin_calc, NA),
         AssetTurnover_calc = ifelse(is.finite(AssetTurnover_calc), AssetTurnover_calc, NA),
         FinancialLeverage_calc = ifelse(is.finite(FinancialLeverage_calc), FinancialLeverage_calc, NA))

duPont %>%
select(Ticker, ROE, ProfitMargin, AssetTurnover, FinancialLeverage, ROE_calc,

STUDENT RESPONSE REQUIRED
We calculated the four DuPont ratios directly from the raw financial statement values: Net Income, Revenues, Total Assets, and Shareholder Equity. These calculated columns (ROE_calc, ProfitMargin_calc, AssetTurnover_calc, FinancialLeverage_calc) ensure full transparency and allow us to verify data accuracy. These new _calc fields align closely with the original values, but we prefer using our computed values to ensure consistency and transparency. No original ratio columns (like ROE, ProfitMargin, etc.) were used — only raw financials.

B. Now that you are confident in the calculated values, let’s remove any outlying data from ROE_calc, ProfitMargin_calc, AssetTurnover_calc, FinancialLeverage_calc. We will use the definition that any value that is beyond 4 standard deviations from the mean of the entire distribution should be thrown out (set to NA). Store these values within your data frame using ROE_clean, ProfitMargin_clean, AssetTurnover_clean, FinancialLeverage_clean.

Question B, Student 
remove_outliers <- function(x) {
  limit <- 4 * sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  x[abs(x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) > limit] <- NA
  return(x)}

duPont <- duPont %>%
  mutate(ROE_clean = remove_outliers(ROE_calc),
         ProfitMargin_clean = remove_outliers(ProfitMargin_calc),
         AssetTurnover_clean = remove_outliers(AssetTurnover_calc),
         FinancialLeverage_clean = remove_outliers(FinancialLeverage_calc))

duPont %>% select(Ticker, `ROE_clean`, `ProfitMargin_clean`, `AssetTurnover_clean`, `FinancialLeverage_clean`) %>% head(7) %>% gt()

C. As a final review let’s examine the acceptable bounds for our analysis, let’s say

  • when ROE_clean is less than zero it should be set to zero (0),
  • when ProfitMargin_clean < -80, it is set to -80, and when ProfitMargin_clean > +80, it is set to +80

Make these changes to the original _clean dataset.

Question C, Student 
duPont <- duPont %>%
  mutate(ROE_clean = ifelse(ROE_clean < 0, 0, ROE_clean),
         ProfitMargin_clean = case_when(ProfitMargin_clean < -80 ~ -80,
                                        ProfitMargin_clean > 80 ~ 80,
                                        TRUE ~ ProfitMargin_clean)) %>%
  mutate(
    ROE_clean = ifelse(is.finite(ROE_clean), ROE_clean, NA),
    ProfitMargin_clean = ifelse(is.finite(ProfitMargin_clean), ProfitMargin_clean, NA),
    AssetTurnover_clean = ifelse(is.finite(AssetTurnover_clean), AssetTurnover_clean, NA),
    FinancialLeverage_clean = ifelse(is.finite(FinancialLeverage_clean), FinancialLeverage_clean, NA))

duPont %>% select(Ticker, ROE_clean,ProfitMargin_clean) %>% head(7) %>% gt()

Analysis follow up: Looking back at your answers in part II, were these results in line with your industry expectations?

STUDENT RESPONSE REQUIRED
Looking back at my answers in Part II, the results from the boxplots are largely consistent with my expectations across industries. For instance, Finance and Technology industries demonstrate the highest median Return on Equity (ROE), which aligns with the assumption that financial institutions benefit from high leverage while tech firms enjoy strong profit margins. The Profit Margin Ratio was also highest in Technology, supporting the view that companies like Apple operate with wide margins due to brand strength and pricing power. In contrast, Consumer Services and Transportation showed the highest Asset Turnover Ratios, which fits the expectation that these industries rely on operational efficiency and rapid asset utilization—evident in companies like Starbucks and Southwest Airlines. Lastly, the Financial Leverage Ratio was most pronounced in Finance and Public Utilities, reflecting their capital-intensive nature and use of debt financing. Overall, the boxplots validated my initial expectations and reinforced the usefulness of the DuPont components for distinguishing financial strengths across industries.

  1. Which industry has seen the greatest improvement in ROE from 2013 to 2015? Consider both the mean and median trends from 2013 to 2015. Create a chart to show the ROE for each industry over time.
Question 02, Student 
library(tidyr)

duPont %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(2013, 2015)) %>%
  group_by(Industry, Year) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_ROE = mean(ROE_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_ROE = median(ROE_clean, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(mean_ROE, median_ROE), names_to = "Metric", values_to = "ROE") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Year, y = ROE, color = Industry)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~Metric, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "ROE Trends by Industry (Mean & Median)", y = "ROE", x = "Year")

Analysis follow up: How many industries have an improvment between 2013 & 2015.

Industries with improvement from 2013 to 2015: Mean ROE Increased:Consumer Services, Finance, Public Utilities Median ROE Increased:Consumer Services, Capital Goods, Finance

Between 2013 and 2015, two industries—Consumer Services and Finance—showed a consistent improvement in both mean and median Return on Equity (ROE). This indicates a robust and steady enhancement in financial performance across companies within these sectors.

While other industries showed improvement in either the mean or the median, only Consumer Services and Finance demonstrated gains across both metrics. This dual improvement suggests that not only did the average ROE rise (which can be influenced by outliers), but the typical company in these industries also experienced better returns, as reflected in the median increase.

This outcome signals that these industries may have been implementing more effective operational or financial strategies during this period, leading to healthier profitability relative to shareholder equity. ]{style=“color: green;”}

STUDENT RESPONSE REQUIRED
While Technology has the highest number of companies in the dataset with 30 firms, it is not the industry with the highest total shareholder equity. That distinction goes to Finance, which, despite having only 29 companies, reports the largest total shareholder equity at over $1.3 trillion. This contrast suggests that companies in the Finance sector tend to operate with significantly larger equity bases — such as major banks and financial institutions — compared to industries like Technology or Consumer Services. Overall, this outcome aligns with expectations: financial firms often manage vast capital reserves and assets, which inflates their equity figures, even if their representation in the dataset is similar to other industries.
